Deco Symmetry 2

GeometryTrianglesArea
Game: This drawing cuts a triangle into three pieces that slide and turn into its mirror image with only two cuts.
How to play: Drag the three corner dots, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Press Move them to watch the pieces turn into place.
Look for the math

A mirror image swaps left and right, so it looks as if you would have to turn pieces over. This applet shows a way to avoid every flip: one set of two cuts works for any triangle at all.

Two cuts from the largest angle

Put A at the biggest corner of the triangle ABC. Drop the altitude AD onto the opposite side, and mark the midpoints E of AB and F of AC. Cut along DE and DF. The three pieces are EBD, the four-cornered piece FAED, and FDC. The page's claim — "It can be done in just two cuts" — is exactly that these three pieces always work, and the logic test confirms it on more than nine hundred triangles, including acute, right and obtuse ones.

Why the middle piece has four corners

The earlier applet Two Symmetric Triangles Are Directly Equidecomposable cuts the same triangle into four pieces: it keeps EBD and FDC but splits the middle along AD into EDA and FAD. For acute triangles it also has a "special acute" switch that uses the circumcenter instead. This second applet has neither switch: joining EDA and FAD into the quadrilateral FAED removes one cut, so the same recipe works in every case.

Turning, never flipping

The dotted line is the mirror. It sends a point (x, y) to (W − x, y), so each piece on the right has the opposite winding to its twin on the left. Listing the vertices backwards — EBD to E′D′B′, for instance — cancels that reversal. A rotation through the signed angle between the first edges, followed by a slide, then carries every vertex onto its twin. That is direct congruence: matching shapes with the same handedness, never a reflection. Press Show hint for the right-angle mark that makes the construction tick.

Why D stays on the side

Because A is the largest corner, the other two corners are at most right angles, so the foot D always falls between B and C. The pieces therefore fill the original triangle exactly: their areas add to the whole, and the same three areas fill the mirror triangle. The logic test checks both partitions and every rotation; the animation here rounds the same motion to the screen's pixels.

Try dragging a corner past a right angle, then press Move them again: the cut still works and no piece ever turns over.
